quote: Verallgemeinerung des Gordanschen Problems eine Form $6^{\text{ten}}$ Grades als Summe eines Quadrates und einer dritten Potenz dar- zustellen: $f = \varphi^m \psi^n + \chi^\sigma \rho^\mu$ \quad $f' = \varphi'^m \psi'^n$
english: Generalisation of Gordan's problem of representing a form of degree 6 as the sum of a square and a cube: f = φ^m ψ^n + χ^σ ρ^μ, f' = φ'^m ψ'^n.
topic: A list of research ideas in invariant theory: groups of operations arising from irrational covariants, covariants defined by vanishing transvectants of binary forms of degree 7 and 10, a generalisation of Gordan's problem on sextic forms, vanishing transvectants of a form with its transform, re-proving a theorem of the dissertation by infinitesimal transformations, and a Lagrange problem on solving a binary form equal to a power of 2 in integers.

triage.modern_statement: Gordan's (and Clebsch's) classical problem asks: given a general binary sextic f(x,y), write f = A^3 + B^2, where A is a binary quadratic and B is a binary cubic. Does such a decomposition exist, how many are there, and how can they be found using invariants and covariants? Hilbert's note generalises the target shape to a sum of two products of powers of forms, f = φ^m ψ^n + χ^σ ρ^μ. The degrees must add up correctly, i.e. m·deg φ + n·deg ψ = σ·deg χ + μ·deg ρ = deg f. In modern terms this asks when a general binary form of degree d lies in the image of the map (φ,ψ,χ,ρ) ↦ φ^m ψ^n + χ^σ ρ^μ, and, if that image is finite-to-one onto the space of forms, how many such decompositions a form has. The extra line f' = φ'^m ψ'^n is not explained on the page. It may mean a degenerate or transformed version where only one summand is left, but that is a guess, so the exact intended setup is only partly clear.
triage.answered_by: No source found that answers Hilbert's general product-of-powers version. Work on closely related special cases: Clebsch (1870) showed a general binary sextic can be written as a cube plus a square. Reznick (arXiv 1203.5722, Pacific J. Math.) treats new canonical forms built from intermediate powers, including a theorem on general binary sextics. A. Patel ('Counting sums of two powers', arXiv 2507.08337, 2025) generalises Clebsch's count to sums of two powers g^a + h^b. Fröberg–Ottaviani–Shapiro (PNAS 2012), Lundqvist–Oneto–Reznick–Shapiro (arXiv 1711.05014) and Reznick (arXiv 2002.00888) study the related Waring problem of writing forms as sums of k-th powers of forms. None of the sources found deals with the mixed products φ^m ψ^n + χ^σ ρ^μ.

evidence.claim: Patel's 2025 paper sets out to generalise Clebsch's result that a general binary sextic can be written as the sum of a cube and a square, i.e. Gordan's problem.
Reznick gives new canonical forms for binary forms that use intermediate powers, including a theorem on writing a general binary sextic in such a form.
Fröberg, Ottaviani and Shapiro set up a Waring problem for polynomial rings: writing forms as sums of k-th powers of forms of lower degree.
Every binary sextic can be written as a sum of at most three cubes of binary quadratic forms (maximal 3-rank of sextics).
Reznick studies which binary sextics are a sum of two cubes of quadratics, and in how many ways, noting that every sextic is a sum of three cubes in infinitely many ways.

triage.why: The base problem is clearly identifiable: a binary sextic as a quadratic cubed plus a cubic squared, associated with Gordan and Clebsch. The modern study of decomposing binary forms into sums of powers is active: Reznick, Fröberg–Ottaviani–Shapiro, Lundqvist–Oneto–Reznick–Shapiro, and Patel in 2025, whose paper explicitly generalises the sextic cube-plus-square case. Hilbert's specific generalisation, sums of two products of powers φ^m ψ^n + χ^σ ρ^μ, is not one of his published problems. I found no source that states or solves it in this generality. The meaning of the f' line is also unclear. My search was cut short by the tool's usage limit before I could check the classical Gordan/Clebsch papers or later literature on products of powers. So 'possibly_unexplored' here means only that this search did not find it, not that it has definitely never been studied.
